slides.0.title: The AVA system and labels
slides.0.subtitle: Definition, percentages and Oregon state law
slides.1.title: What an AVA is
slides.1.highlights.0.title: The first AVA
slides.1.highlights.0.content: Augusta, Missouri became the first federally established viticultural area on 20 June 1980
slides.1.highlights.1.title: The authority
slides.1.highlights.1.content: The ATF defined AVAs from 1980; from January 2003, under the Homeland Security Act, the TTB took over
slides.1.highlights.2.title: AVAs can nest
slides.1.highlights.2.content: An AVA can sit inside a larger one, and wineries generally use the most specific AVA that applies
slides.1.content: An AVA defines only a geographical area, not varieties or winemaking — its biggest difference from a European AOC.
slides.2.title: Federal labelling percentages
slides.2.highlights.0.title: Origin percentages
slides.2.highlights.0.content: At least 85% of the grapes must come from the named AVA, and at least 75% for a state or county; the wine must be fully finished in the state
slides.2.highlights.1.title: Variety and vintage
slides.2.highlights.1.content: A varietal label requires an appellation, and the US minimum is 75% of the variety. Vintage: 85% with an AVA, 75% with only a state, county or country
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Estate bottled
slides.2.highlights.2.content: Requires 100% of grapes from land the winery owns or controls, with winery and vineyard inside the AVA and the wine crushed, fermented, aged and bottled on the premises
slides.2.content: Remember three numbers: AVA 85, state/county 75, variety 75.
slides.3.title: Oregon's state law
slides.3.highlights.0.title: 90% for varieties
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Oregon requires at least 90% of the variety (for example Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Pinot Gris)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Exceptions
slides.3.highlights.1.content: About 18 varieties are exempt and follow the federal 75%, including Cabernet Sauvignon, Sauvignon Blanc and Syrah
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Oregon origin
slides.3.highlights.2.content: When Oregon, a county or an Oregon AVA is named, 100% of the grapes must be from Oregon and 95% from the named appellation
slides.3.content: Oregon is stricter than federal law: 95% for the appellation and 90% for varieties (with exceptions).
